fact: An instruction is usually made up of a combination of an operation code and some way of specifying an operand, most commonly by its location or address in memory
Instruction format is the layout of bits in an instruction, for example 11100011111110000001110000 is ADD R1,R2
An instruction is divided into opcode, which is the function, operands, which may be implicit or explicit, and the addressing mode
Instructions typically have 0, 1, 2 or 3 operands, and there is usually more than one instruction format in an instruction set

The format of an instruction is usually depicted in a rectangular box symbolizing the bits of the instruction as they appear in memory words or in a control register, and the bits are divided into groups called fields
The most common fields found in instruction formats are the Opcode, the Mode, and the Address or Operand

The operation code field specifies the operation to be performed, the address field designates a memory address or a processor register, and the mode field specifies the way the operand or the effective address is determined
In the simple 16-bit instruction format example the fields are Opcode of 4 bits, Register of 4 bits and Address of 8 bits
In the 16-bit format the 4-bit opcode defines the operation such as ADD or SUB, the 4-bit register specifies a register such as R1 or R2, and the 8-bit address gives the memory location
In the binary example 1010 0011 11001010 the opcode 1010 is ADD, the register 0011 is R3 and the address 11001010 is 202, so the interpretation is ADD R3, [202]

In the 32-bit binary example 000001 00001 00010 00011 00000000000, the opcode 000001 is ADD, R1 is 00001 as destination, R2 is 00010 as operand 1 and R3 is 00011 as operand 2, so the interpretation is ADD R1, R2, R3
The instruction format examples are studied through an assembly language program that evaluates X equals A plus B, times C plus D, used to understand the 3, 2, 1 and 0 address formats
The three-address program for X equals A plus B times C plus D is ADD R1, A, B then ADD R2, C, D then MUL X, R1, R2, where M[A] denotes the operand at the memory address symbolized by A

The advantage of the three-address format is that it results in short programs when evaluating arithmetic expressions, and the disadvantage is that the binary-coded instructions require too many bits to specify three addresses
Two-address instructions are the most common in commercial computers, and each address field can specify either a processor register or a memory word
The two-address program for X equals A plus B times C plus D is MOV R1, A then ADD R1, B then MOV R2, C then ADD R2, D then MOL R1, R2 then MOV X, R1

The MOV instruction moves or transfers the operands to and from memory and processor registers, and the first symbol listed in a two-address instruction is assumed to be both a source and the destination where the result is transferred
One-address instructions use an implied accumulator register, AC, for all data manipulation, and for multiplication and division there is a need for a second register
The one-address program for X equals A plus B times C plus D is LOAD A, ADD B, STORE T, LOAD C, ADD D, MOL T, STORE X
In the one-address format all operations are done between the AC register and a memory operand, and T is the address of a temporary memory location required for storing the intermediate result

A stack-organized computer does not use an address field for the instructions ADD and MUL, but the PUSH and POP instructions do need an address field to specify the operand that communicates with the stack
The zero-address program for X equals A plus B times C plus D is PUSH A, PUSH B, ADD, PUSH C, PUSH D, ADD, MOL, POP X, where TOS stands for top of stack
To evaluate arithmetic expressions in a stack computer it is necessary to convert the expression into reverse Polish notation
The name zero-address is given to this type of computer because of the absence of an address field in the computational instructions

The revision class repeats that instruction format is the layout of bits in an instruction, that an instruction divides into opcode, operands and addressing mode, that instructions typically have 0, 1, 2 or 3 operands, and that there is usually more than one instruction format in an instruction set
The revision class repeats that the bits of an instruction are divided into groups called fields and that the most common fields are Opcode, Mode, and Address or Operand

The revision exercise asks for zero, one, two and three address instruction formats for a Pentium 4 assembly language program segment evaluating X equals A times B, plus C over D, all divided by F times G plus J times K
In the revision worked answer the three-address version is MUL R1, A, B then DIV R2, C, D then ADD R1, R1, R2 then MUL R2, F, G then MUL R3, J, K then ADD R2, R2, R3 then DIV X, R2, R3
In the revision worked answer the zero-address version begins PUSH A, PUSH B, MUL, PUSH C, PUSH D, DIV, ADD and ends with POP X
